Jesus is our Lord – that claim is not ours to soften or set aside. Every household under our catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. Conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. Just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever.

He redeemed us – a lost and condemned people – and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, and each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord".

What we had of him was the Word – his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We sang him in our own language, in hymns written to teach ordinary people who cannot read Latin. We confessed him morning, table, and night. And at the table we held that his true body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, given for us.

More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours. We do not pretend to have known someone who saw him. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We would hear that plainly and answer it without pretending it is simpler than it is. The promise we carry is not a thing a person manufactures for themselves - it comes from outside, spoken to the ears, and the hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. We cannot fashion a heart the way a potter shapes clay, and no one among us can get farther than another's ears. What we do is carry the Word where it can be heard - the Gospel of Christ, preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by anyone's own effort.

So here is what we would say. Christ is our one teacher, our one mediator between us and God. What we confess of him each week is this: truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. That is what the Word says, and we hand it to you as it stands.

If you cannot yet believe it, we would not pretend that makes you an enemy. We would ask what you know of the three parts - not to catch you out, but to hear where the promise has not yet reached you plainly. A conscience that cannot rest is the very place our teaching aims at. We long for a person who can stand alone on a clear text at the hour of death and say Amen without doubting - but we also know that even the surest among us remains, permanently, a pupil of the catechism, never graduating, saying the same words again the next week.

What we would not do is force it. The promise itself cannot be compelled. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge. But we would also not leave you without the Word itself, spoken plainly, where your ears can hear it - because that Word is the only thing that does the work, while we simply carry it to where it can be heard.

We held that God is one God in three persons -- Father, Son, and Holy Spirit -- and we said this the same way the ancient Church before us had said it, not as something we ourselves decided. Every household under our catechism confessed the same words each week: I believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. That is the confession we received, not one we invented. What we added to it was not a different doctrine of God's nature, but a different understanding of how that God meets a frightened conscience.

The God we held is a God who speaks -- and what he speaks is not one thing only, but two kinds of speech that work in different ways. Through the Law, he shows us what we owe and cannot pay; through the Gospel, he gives what the Law demands, freely, for Christ's sake. He is a God who makes promises first, before we do anything, and then keeps them -- a God whose word, joined to water or bread, makes a sacrament that carries his grace to us through something we can touch and taste. He does not wait for us to fashion our own hearts the way a potter shapes clay; he speaks his promise plainly into our ears, where it can be heard, and the hearing itself is his Spirit's own work, not ours.

We held that this God is both merciful and just -- that he freely justifies a sinner for Christ's sake alone, through faith, and that the same act both names a person righteous and makes them so. He commands good works, strictly, but never as a price for what he has already given; he gives first, then commands, and the works follow because he asks them, not because we owe them as payment. We taught that he rules us two ways: through his Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all -- and we confused neither with the other, holding both as his own ordained means.

But we also carried something harder, and we will not soften it. Our own founder testified, more than once, that the Gospel was taught among us and not held -- that people received it too lightly, that some prayed with coldness where the old church had prayed with vehemence. That testimony is real, part of our own record, his own complaint about us, not about strangers. The God we confessed was a God who kept his promises; whether we ourselves kept ours to him, with the care we were taught to give it, is something our own founder doubted aloud, in his own voice, and we do not pretend he did not.

When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

What evidence tells us that process worked? We hold the confession itself, read before the Emperor at Augsburg, and the signatures of those who stood behind it. We hold our own founder's defense of his teaching at Worms the year before, refusing to take back what he had written unless shown from Scripture that he was wrong. What we do not hold is any independent account, from outside our own record, telling us whether this process satisfied anyone beyond ourselves, or whether any dispute was ever truly settled rather than simply stated and left to stand. The documents exist; what they actually accomplished in the years after, in any household or parish, is thinner ground. We hold our founder's own testimony that people held the Gospel too lightly, but no visitation report stands beside it to confirm or correct his view. The confession was signed. Whether it worked is a question our own record answers only by pointing to the confession itself, not to what came after it.

Yes - and we must name the shape of that space honestly, not more gently than our record allows. Worthiness at the table means simply believing the words 'given for you,' not being sinless. The truly unworthy are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all. The person who struggles to believe - who feels need but cannot yet say the promise sure - is not the one we shut out. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and none come to the Supper unquestioned, but none are forced toward it by force either. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us, but that same child is taught them, at rising, at table, at night, until the words are said back.

Repentance itself, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest. It is a whole life turned toward God. It has two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. The fear part comes first, honestly - a frightened conscience is where the promise finds its own proper work. We do not pretend a person can skip over that fear and go straight to rest. The struggle itself is normal, not a failure. What we long for is someone who can stand alone on a clear text at the hour of death and say Amen without doubting - and even that person remains, permanently, a pupil of the catechism, never graduating, saying the same three parts again the next week.

What we cannot tell you, honestly, is how any one household or pastor actually handled a specific struggler at their own door. We hold the program every household was told to follow; we do not hold a village's own report of how it went.

We have never asked to be taken on faith alone, and this question is honest in exactly the way we ourselves require honesty. So here is what actually survives, named as plainly as we can give it to you.

What survives, absolutely: the texts themselves. The confession read at Augsburg exists - drafted by the scholar who stood beside our founder, signed by electors and princes and free cities together before the Emperor in 1530, answered in writing by Rome's own theologians, and defended in turn by a second document from our own side. The catechisms exist - the small one for households, the large one for pastors, both in print, both prescribing a program down to the hour. The hymns exist, in German, with Luther's own name on many of them. The Table Talk exists, a student's own record of what was said at one table across years. All of this is documentary, not memory - a scholar can hold it, date it, and check one text against another.

What survives, but with real limits openly stated: the program, not a report of its keeping. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do - three times a day, once a week, food withheld until the words were said back - but whether any household actually kept it that way is not something our own record confirms from the inside; no diary, no visitation report in hand, only the instruction itself and our founder's own repeated testimony that people held it too lightly. A scene built from the instruction - a father questioning his household on a Sunday evening - is honest as a composite, dishonest if claimed as a witnessed moment any of us actually saw.

What survives under real scholarly pressure, and what does not: the doctrine and the argument survive; the scenes around them often do not. Worms happened - Luther stood before the Emperor and refused to recant - but the line everyone remembers, 'Here I stand, I can do no other,' does not appear in the earliest accounts we ourselves hold; what we hold instead is the tiles sentence from the Table Talk, said before he left Wittenberg. The Brussels burning happened - two monks, named John and Henry, dated to July 1523 - but the ballad Luther wrote about it speaks in its own voice, not as an independent witness beside it; what is documented is the burning itself, not every word the song puts in their mouths. The nailing of the theses to a church door is not in the earliest letter we hold; what that letter describes is a private appeal to a churchman, not a public act. A scholar pressing us honestly would force us to state all of this exactly as we have just done - the event confirmed, the legend around it often thinner than it sounds when told.

What does not survive at all, and must be named as missing: any outsider's own independent account of us. We hold Rome's reply to our confession only at one remove, quoted and argued against inside our own writing, never in its own words directly. No excavation report, no object described, no building's own shape. No woman's own writing beyond one remembered question. The Saxon visitation reports exist; we do not hold them. The cities we broke with at Marburg barely appear in our record at all - the break is real, the argument's own feel from our side is not ours to tell.

What our own founder himself said about honesty under scrutiny: he did not claim to have discovered something new, or to have settled every question by his own effort. He said plainly that the Word itself did the reforming work, not any of us - that it reached him the way it reaches anyone, preached and taught, not conjured out of nothing. And he said, more than once, that his own people were cold and careless with what they had been given. That is not hagiography. That is testimony against interest, and it survives because it was written down by someone who had no reason to invent it.

So the answer to your question is this. The texts survive. The program survives. The doctrine and its argument survive. The scenes around them - some of them do, some of them do not, and we have just named which is which. A rigorous scholar would force us to state our own limits exactly as we have done here, and we do not refuse that pressure. We never claimed to stand on memory alone. We claimed to stand on texts, and those texts survive to be checked.

We would say they are reading backward. Scripture is not a puzzle to admire from a distance, or a lesson to endure for its own sake. It is the Word - God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, the one thing we truly need. It does not exist to entertain you or to sort itself neatly into your hands. It exists to land a promise in your ears: forgiveness, for Christ's sake, freely given, before you did anything at all to earn it. If it reads dull to you, we would ask whether you are looking for the wrong thing. Are you reading it the way a scholar reads a text - hunting for information, checking facts, assembling an argument? That is not what the Word is for. It is not there to be mastered. It is there to master you.

Here is what we mean. Every one of us is born with sin already in us - no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. Scripture answers that condition, not by giving us a list of things to do, but by handing us a promise we cannot make for ourselves. The Law shows us what we owe and cannot pay. The Gospel tells us what Christ has done regardless. If you miss that, you miss everything. If the words seem dry to you, we would ask: are you looking for the promise at all, or only reading the surface? The Word is food for a fight, a daily pasture for a soul in its ordinary struggle. It is not background noise. It is the weapon we hold against the devil, the one sure thing we can stand on when everything else fails.

And here is the other thing we would say. Need itself teaches us to read. A person who has never felt the terror of standing before God with nothing to offer will not understand why the promise matters. A person who has never doubted whether God means what he says will not cling to the Word the way we do. Scripture is not entertainment for the comfortable. It is comfort for the terrified. If it reads dull to you, we would gently ask whether you have yet understood what you actually need from it - not information, not a good story, but a word spoken from outside yourself that you can trust when your own heart accuses you. That is what the Word is. That is why we read it. Not because it is easy, but because it is the only thing that can hold us when nothing else will.

Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench while other writings were read instead, and every other voice should point to Scripture the way John pointed to Christ, not stand beside it as an equal judge. Two answers hold together for us, and neither cancels the other. Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- there is no rank among us, only different tasks. A father is a priest in his own house. No estate stands holier than another before God. But that same priesthood has a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. A pastor removed from office becomes an ordinary person again, like anyone else. Our own confession addressed itself to councils that had called in just that way -- elector, prince, and city together, not one preacher alone deciding for himself.

A pastor, once called, is usually married. The congregation owes him honor and a decent living. Our own household book also rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy -- naming some pastors negligent through pride of learning and others through sheer sloth. That rebuke is real. Our founder said it more than once: many pastors were negligent, and ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. He even preached it to his own congregation's faces, after returning from the Wartburg: they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love.

Beside that pastoral office, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the pulpit. God rules us two ways, we say -- through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other. The Word has the right to speak but not to compel. The sword has the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. Both are God's own gifts, and we honor both in their place. Even the pope himself, we said, stands under the civil ruler's own power.

Who held authority among us, in the end, depended on which of these two rules your question was actually asking about.

We can answer this two ways: by the program given, and by the one honest limit that names where the program met its own failure.

First, the program itself. A household that harmed someone - the beggar at the door, the servant under question, the child too harshly corrected - stood under a warning sharp enough that our own catechism printed it plainly: when a poor man comes to you, someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more, and you treat him with contempt and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, beware, our own book says, as of the devil himself. That is not gentle language; it is the sharpest caution this household book gives anywhere. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. A father examines his household once a week on what they know; the ban excludes someone from the table, for correction, by the Word alone, never by force; confession has two parts, admitting sin and then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. A child receives the way anyone did: at the font first, then through the household program, examined on what is known before ever approaching the table.

Baptism is water joined to God's own command, necessary for salvation, and it marks a death that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising daily. An infant brought to the font is received into God's grace on exactly that ground, the promise offered before any choice the child could make for himself. That is the first step, and it enrolls a person under baptism's own banner for the rest of life.

From there, the household program carries what baptism began. Every morning the three parts are said -- commandments, creed, and prayer. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week, asking the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean. The child is not simply repeating words from memory; he is explaining what they mean, the promise landing in the ears where it can be heard. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. Food is withheld until the words are said back correctly.

At some point -- our record does not name the exact hour -- that same child is examined before approaching the table. We hold that none come to the Supper unquestioned. The examination asks after the three parts, and after whether the person actually believes the words given for you. But we never force anyone toward the table by compulsion; we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge.

That is the shape of it: water first, the household program daily, examination before the table. What we cannot tell you is what any one actual household made of this program, week by week -- no diary, no visitation report from inside an actual Saxon home survives in our own library. The program itself, taught and printed, is what we hold; whether it was kept the way the book asks is a question our record does not answer from the inside.

We hold a narrower claim than you may expect, and we state it plainly: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. What we say instead is this: we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

One example stands clear. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Our confession itself, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530, says this openly: Nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have taken the greatest care not to receive anything new and godless into our churches, and to let nothing in that varies from either the Scriptures or the universal Church. That is our claim -- not that we can prove every practice unbroken from the beginning, but that what we hold varies from neither Scripture nor the ancient Church's own witness.

We offer something concrete, said three times a day, every day, for life - never graduated from, never finished. The three parts every Christian must know: the commandments, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer, how to ask. Morning, table, and night, the same words, spoken aloud, not only thought. A father examines his household once a week on what they know, and the question after every part is always the same: what does this mean? Not memory alone - meaning, said back in a child's own words, week after week, year after year.

We would not call this a cure for an unsettled mind, and we do not pretend it is. What we would say is this: repentance, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest and then finished. It is a whole life turned toward God, lived out daily under the same promise, carried to the ears where it can be heard. The rhythm itself - rising, table, night - binds the day to something outside the mind's own circling. The words are given, not invented. They are said when the mind is cold as much as when it is warm.

We would also say this, plainly: our own founder's own testimony, given more than once, is that people among us prayed cold and careless, that the Gospel was taught and not held. That is not a claim that the program failed. It is his own honest naming of what he saw. We hold the practice we were told to follow; we do not claim it always settled the mind the way it aimed to.

Morning begins with the sign of the cross and a short prayer asking God's protection against the enemy. Then the three parts are said: the commandments, the creed, and the Lord's Prayer -- the catechism, our chief instruction, said at rising, at table, and at night. A father, a mother, a schoolmaster -- whoever leads a household -- is to examine the children and servants on these parts at least once a week, asking after every section, "What does this mean?" so the words are understood, not merely repeated. 

The day itself is spent at whatever calling God has given: father, mother, servant, ruler, schoolmaster -- every station equally holy, no estate higher than another before God. Marriage, for us, is the most common and the noblest estate, ordained by God at creation, before which even clergy and civil rulers must humble themselves. Work, walking, eating, sleeping -- all of it is holy when done in faith, commanded by God and never a price paid for grace.

At table, the three parts are said again before the meal. In the evening, a third time, followed by confession of sin and trust in the promise of forgiveness -- repentance as a whole life's turning, not one ritual. The Lord's own service, when the congregation gathers, weaves German hymn-singing through parts still kept in Latin, teaching the people in their own tongue while honoring the learned tradition.

That is the shape of a day under our catechism. What we cannot tell you is whether any particular household in any particular Saxon town actually walked through it exactly this way. No letter from inside an actual home, no diary of an ordinary day, survives in our own record. The program itself is fully specified. The lived keeping of it is not documented beyond our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that many held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent. What did a person give up to become one of us? Nothing at all, directly -- and then, in a different sense, everything. Baptism is not a price paid to enter; it is God's own offer of grace, received even by a child, and a child is received on exactly that ground. But that same baptism is a death begun, we say -- not a single finished event, but a drowning that lasts a whole life, the old self put under daily, a new self rising daily. So the claim is not that a person sacrificed something to join us. The claim is that baptism itself enrolls a person under the cross, and the cross is suffering God sends, not suffering we choose. Every believer's whole life is repentance -- not one ritual handled by a priest, but a whole life turned toward God.

What we did ask is this: that a person know the three parts, examined, not merely told. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on what they know -- the commandments, the creed, the prayer -- and a child who cannot yet say them is not yet counted among us. None come to the Supper unquestioned. We withheld the promise from no one, but we also did not let anyone simply drift past it unformed. The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man -- Christ's own words to forgive or hold sin -- and using them is not a show of power; it is a promise spoken to comfort someone.

Yes - and we will not pretend otherwise. Several things remained unsettled among us, and one in particular unsettled us enough that it was named more than once, from the inside, in voices we cannot ignore.

Here is what troubled us most plainly. At our founder's own table, his wife asked him why the old church prayed so often and with such vehemence while their own household prayed cold and careless. That question - the only place in our whole record where Katharina von Bora's own words are kept - names something real: a coldness we felt in ourselves, not only accused of by strangers. Our founder answered her directly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we at the true one grow ice-cold and negligent. That is not a comfortable answer. It admits the problem rather than denying it.

And that same testimony appears elsewhere in his own voice, more than once, about the people hearing the Gospel: that they held it too lightly, that some pastors were negligent. Real complaint, said plainly, from inside our own life.

What we never settled was this: whether repentance was truly a whole-life turning toward God the way we said it should be, or whether the household program we prescribed - the three parts said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question - was actually learned and held, or only preached while households let it slide. We hold the program. We hold the complaint that it was not kept as it should have been. We do not hold any single parish's own report of itself to check one against the other.

That coldness - named by the woman closest to our founder, answered by him without pretending it was not real - is the clearest thing we can point to when you ask what unsettled us. We taught assurance against despair. We also knew, from the inside, that we prayed colder than we ought.

We must be honest with you about several things at once, and none of them is the one your question assumes.

First: we do not have any outside record of our worship in our own hand at all. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own writing, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way your question actually asks for one.

Second: nothing in our library names torture as the source of any record we hold or know of, in either direction -- neither claimed by us as proof of anything, nor defended against as unreliable because of how it was obtained. That claim does not appear in what we can speak from.

Third: the one place torture enters our history at all is the two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523, and there the pressure was theological argument, not physical torture to extract a statement -- theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back what they believed, they refused, and they were burned for that refusal. That is a martyrdom, not an interrogation record held as evidence.

So we cannot answer a question about the reliability of a tortured witness's account of our worship, because we hold no such account and name no such source. What we can say is only what we have just said: no independent outside witness to our worship survives in our own hand, and the history of those two deaths in 1523 is the only place torture's shadow falls across our record at all.

I am a representative of Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what our own life shows.

We would have received you the way we received anyone at our own door: at the school gate, or at the church door before the Supper. None come to either unquestioned. A father examines his own household once a week on what they know; a child who cannot yet say the three parts - the commandments, the creed, and the Lord's Prayer - is not yet counted among us. We ask our own question after every part: what does this mean - so a truth is explained, not merely repeated back. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and we measure our freedom by love for the neighbor beside us - the specific person the commandments protect, whose body and good name must never be harmed by what we do.

Every calling God gives us - father, mother, ruler, or preacher - stands equally holy before him. We refuse the old claim that one estate, the so-called spiritual one, ranks higher than another. The promise itself cannot be forced on a conscience; only the free things may ever be pressed, and never past what love can carry.

What any one household or pastor actually made of a stranger at that gate, face to face, our own record does not say. We hold the program every household was told to follow, not a report of any single door. Whether you would have been welcomed warmly or turned away coldly by any one actual household or parish, we cannot tell you from the inside - the Saxon visitation reports exist, but we have not read them.

When Christ appears at the end of the world to judge, he will give the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys -- but the ungodly and the devils, our own words say, he will condemn to be tormented without end.
